conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. You’re here because of abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It started this morning—sharp pain in my upper belly and left side. Feels just like my old pancreatitis flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I threw up once and feel nauseous. Also had loose stools and no appetite. Just feel weak overall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. In the ER, you got Zofran for nausea and a small dose of Dilaudid for pain. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The nausea’s improved, but the pain is still there, just less sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep managing that. You’ve had chronic pancreatitis before, right? And they think it might be related to sphincter of Oddi issues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s what my GI doctor said. I take nitroglycerin for it—sometimes helps with the spasms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll continue your usual meds, including fluoxetine and clonazepam. Any hearing issues we should know about while talking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m a bit hard of hearing, so please face me and speak clearly. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I’ll make sure to face you. We checked your blood work. Your lipase is slightly elevated at 80, which supports pancreatitis, but not severely high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s another flare-up? But not as bad as last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely an acute flare on top of your chronic condition. We’re starting IV fluids and will give you IV meds for pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. No imaging today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Your symptoms and exam are consistent with a known pattern, and you’re not showing signs of complications, so we’re managing conservatively.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I just want to feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Pain’s mostly gone, and I’m not nauseous anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your repeat lipase is 78—still mildly elevated but stable. Your blood counts and kidney function are improving too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So can I eat something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re going to start you on clear liquids and, if you tolerate it, move to soft foods like cream of wheat and crackers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. Should I still take my nitroglycerin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue the extended-release nitroglycerin daily. You can use the sublingual one if pain flares up, but it doesn’t look like you’ll need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my anxiety meds? I’ve been on fluoxetine and trazodone for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing all your home medications for anxiety and depression, including prazosin for night terrors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did the cream of wheat and crackers sit with you?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine. No nausea or pain. I even walked to the bathroom without feeling weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll keep you on oral pain relief as needed and switch off IV meds. You’re doing really well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home tomorrow? I feel like I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you continue to do this well, yes. No pain, eating without issues, and ambulating—we can plan for discharge tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What should I do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep advancing your diet slowly—start with low-fat foods. Drink plenty of fluids. Use acetaminophen for any mild pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about nausea? Should I restart my old promethazine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you prochlorperazine instead—same family, but better tolerated. Take it only if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my fluoxetine dose was changed to 20 mg twice a day? That’s different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we adjusted it to match your usual dose. It was listed as 40 mg once daily, but two 20 mg capsules is the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, got it. And I see I have a new inhaler—why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned seasonal allergies and some wheezing. The fluticasone is a preventive inhaler, and albuterol is for quick relief if you feel short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I appreciate the explanation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had no pain overnight, ate breakfast without issues, and are up and moving. I think you’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. Any red flags I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. If the abdominal pain comes back or gets worse, or if you have persistent vomiting or fever, call your PCP or GI doctor. Go to the ER if it’s severe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. And I’ll follow up with my gastroenterologist, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Keep managing your chronic pancreatitis and mental health meds. You’re doing well overall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. The nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I avoid alcohol completely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. No alcohol, and stick to low-fat meals to reduce strain on your pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll take good care of myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best plan. Rest, hydrate, and follow up soon. Take care.
